title: Back to School: Between the First and Last Day of Class
author: Brandon Crowe
summary: Brandon Crowe, superintendent of Great Hearts Arizona, addresses the central anxiety of classical educators: how can a teacher know their work is actually forming students toward truth, goodness, and beauty when human beings are unpredictable and the fruit of formation is often invisible for years? He rejects two comforting but false beliefs -- that curriculum alone changes people, and that a teacher's will can force virtue -- arguing instead that classical schools must 'trust in the efficacy of ordinary means': the belief that the right content, delivered rightly, by the right people, reliably shapes hearts over time even without guaranteed individual outcomes. The bulk of the piece is a practical account of what that trust looks like day to day -- modeling curiosity and goodwill toward students, colleagues, and parents rather than prejudging them, communicating directly and apologizing when wrong, and demonstrating the intellectual seriousness a school claims to value. Crowe frames the essay as a message meant to bookend the school year, given to teachers both as encouragement at the start and as a reminder of purpose at the end.
points: Rejects the belief that 'the curriculum will change them' on its own, pointing out that history is full of people who studied great books and rejected noble pursuits anyway -- the curriculum is necessary but not sufficient.

Also rejects the belief that teachers can change people 'through the power of our will,' arguing educators can only help, love, and support students in testing ideas, not force internalization of virtue.

Proposes 'trust in the efficacy of ordinary means' as the working philosophy: the right formation, delivered consistently, shapes hearts and minds even though no single interaction guarantees a specific future outcome.

Gives concrete behavioral examples of embodying that trust -- 'come inquiring' rather than assuming, showing genuine curiosity about students' lives, and apologizing openly when a teacher is wrong in a discipline or instructional matter.
quotes: The single biggest challenge we face is one of meaning: how do I know that my work is meaningful, that it actually bears fruit? This is the quandary of every teacher (and parent), and what amplifies the difficulty is the reality that human beings are changeable.
The curriculum is not messianic. Throughout history, how many villains have studied the same great works of literature and philosophy, and yet rejected noble pursuits?
We cannot force people to be better. We can and should limit acting out and misbehavior, but we do not control the heart of another.

Our foundation, then, is rather simple: we trust in the efficacy of ordinary means. What I mean by this is that we believe if we educate students in the right way, it will make a difference for them and ultimately for society.
We don't prejudge our students, colleagues, or parents. We let their actions and words speak for themselves. When something makes us wonder, we ask about it.

The difference you will make cannot be measured today, or tomorrow, or even next year. In fact, I'm not sure it can ever be measured in exactly a way that would satisfy us; that would give us undeniable evidence of success.
